Usually, the Roman governor, in this case the knight Pontius Pilate, was responsible for judicial proceedings, judgment, and execution. Contemporary Roman testimonies, such as the annals of Tacitus or the early Christian author Tertullian (Ad martyras, 2), therefore hold him responsible for the death sentence. The Soviet power had all grain, including seed grain, confiscated; as a result, seven million people starved to death by 1933. text:
Leder's Journal (I): "Nazi Hunters" - Showing what is not to be said

This 17-second sequence of images could be seen on Tuesday, February 15, 2022, in the 8:00 PM edition of the "Tagesschau." In each of the four shots, the text "SOURCE Ministry of Defense Russia" was superimposed in the upper left of the image. The sequence of images was announced with a sentence from an off-screen narrator stating that a report from noon said, "Russia is sending individual troops back to the barracks." The narrator then repeats what is already displayed in writing above: "The ministry publishes these images." The four images form a short film that tells of tanks being maneuvered from a snowy landscape onto a train. Only one image is missing, showing the fully loaded train moving from left to right out of the frame; then the narrative would be complete, that Russia is moving a part of its troops from here to there. But exactly this location is missing, as is a precise determination of the time [Gruppe 1] the images were taken. Dwarfs at a giant's table: On the day the sequence of images could be seen in the "Tagesschau," Federal Chancellor Olaf Scholz (SPD) had visited the Russian President Vladimir Putin. Of their conversation, which is said to have lasted four hours, only a short shot could be seen. Here, one could see that Putin placed his visitor from Germany, as he had done a few days earlier with the French President Emmanuel Macron at a long table, in such a way that guest and host sat far apart. This was justified by the note that Scholz, like Macron, had not been examined for a Corona infection by Russian doctors, but only by their own doctors. However, an imperial gesture also shimmers through the image, with which Putin shows himself less as a host than as someone who assigns others their place. Putin loves such things. At an inauguration many years ago, he walked through the Kremlin for minutes, which a phalanx of cameras were to record live, before he finally reached his office. While the press conference of Putin and Scholz, broadcast live by Phoenix, was still running, the news arrived that the Duma, i.e., the Russian parliament, was demanding that Russia recognize the "People's Republics" that broke away from Ukraine around Donetsk and Luhansk as independent states. In the strictly planned procedures of the Russian nomenklatura, it is inconceivable that Putin did not know this or—to put it differently—had not planned exactly this. That what then became political reality a week later—the recognition of the "People's Republics"—and again two days later on February 24 led to the invasion of Ukraine, was part of a master plan and was thus intended to mislead Olaf Scholz and, through the live broadcast, Germany and the West. This was also the purpose of the film piece, which was intended to prove the term "troop withdrawal" and thus deceive about the real military situation. The lack of own images: The television, which claims to show everything that is important, suffers in these days from a poverty of its own images. Thus, it can only take over and interpret official recordings of staged events, such as the carefully choreographed state visit of Scholz to Putin or the tendentially imperial speeches of the Russian president. And it can show images to which something is attributed by those who distribute them. In the mentioned short film, for example, the claim of a partial withdrawal of Russian troops. The same applies to satellite images presented in the following days which came from Western intelligence services; they were inscribed with the fact that many Russian troops were still stationed around Ukraine. These overview shots also lacked time and location information; furthermore, they would have had to be resolved in detail in order to be able to recognize which troops were involved. The mentioned sequence of images with the tanks, like the satellite photos from the intelligence services, was shown by the television and it adopted the meanings that were inscribed to them; at the same time, it distanced itself from them through the source citation. If one attributes something to an image, such a text is called a "legend." In Latin, this gerundivum designates what is to be read. In medieval Latin, this became a story that was to be believed. Note: Since 2001, media scholar Dietrich Leder has written a "Journal of Images and Tones" for Medienkorrespondenz, in which it was less about individual films than about symptomatic details in which essential elements of staging could be analyzed and interpreted. This journal now finds a new home at filmdienst.de after the closure of Medienkorrespondenz and appears once a month.

An economic crisis would last longer, probably over several years, as Lindner also explained. It could trigger deep structural upheavals in industry, accompanied by losses in prosperity, growth, and jobs. As a result, the state could collect less tax revenue than expected, and the distribution room for social benefits would be smaller.

However, it is not yet that far. In their economic forecasts for the current and coming year, most economists still expect a growing economy, albeit at significantly lower rates than just a few weeks ago. But with every further day of war in Ukraine and every further step by the Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin, who uses his gas as a weapon against [Gruppe 1], Germany moves a little closer to a recession in the second half of the year. By definition, it would already occur if economic output shrinks for two consecutive quarters. Often, such a "technical recession" is hardly noticeable to people if the labor market remains robust and - as is still the case in Germany - no large-scale layoffs are imminent. A deep crisis, on the other hand, would likely be triggered if Putin were to suddenly turn off the gas tap completely. "A profound economic crisis arises from the fact that production structures are no longer marketable on a large scale and must be restructured. This is worse than a conventional recession because such an adjustment crisis lasts longer and is more costly for all of us," says Stefan Kooths, Vice President of the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW). "A loss of secure gas supply for industry would be such a crisis trigger, as would a permanently strong price increase for gas compared to other world regions. Then the pressure to adjust in German industry would be enormously high, as a large part of the chemical industry depends on it. Such a crisis could last for years because the realignment of production takes time. It would be accompanied in particular by production closures and job losses on a larger scale," Kooths predicts.

The German economy is vulnerable to crisis because it already faces enormous challenges, which are now being intensified by the Ukraine war. "We had a golden decade between 2006 and 2016; now we are probably heading towards a lost decade. Because we face a multitude of structural challenges that will weigh on economic growth for a longer period: demographics, decarbonization, deglobalization, and infrastructure deficits have a negative impact," says Andreas Scheuerle, Germany expert at Dekabank. How Transnistria came into being

On July 29, the F.A.Z. published the very readable contribution "Protectorate Russia" by Michael Martens on the topic of Transnistria. Perhaps it should also be mentioned that both the emergence of the territory and its naming occurred long before 1992. The current Republic of Moldova – in somewhat different borders – had been part of Russia for over 100 years when Romanian troops captured the land on the right bank of the Dniester in 1920. To maintain the Soviet Union's claim to Moldova, Stalin arbitrarily formed the Moldavian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic within the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in 1924 from a narrow strip of territory in Ukraine on the left bank of the Dniester. This is how today's Pridnestrovie (land this side of the Dniester), as it calls itself, came into being. In 1940, the Soviet Union again occupied Moldova along with that Ukrainian strip. The Moldavian Soviet Republic was retaken from Romania in 1941 with the help of Hitler's Germany. Further east of that, in western Ukraine with Odessa, Romania established a brutal regime of terror that claimed countless victims, particularly among the Jewish population; this area was called [Gruppe 1] Transnistria (land beyond the Dniester). The world outside transferred the ill-fated name in 1992 to the rebel territory on the left bank of the Dniester.

From 1944 to 1991, Moldova was again part of the Soviet Union. Upon its collapse, the Republic of Moldova, including the Ukrainian strip of territory, became an independent state. Otto Freiherr Grote, Berlin

When Merrick Garland was asked by journalists after three months as American Attorney General about the events in the department under the predecessor government, he replied: “I will not look back.” Many Democrats found this unsatisfying, as they felt a public reckoning was missing. But that is not the style of the 69-year-old centrist. Garland wants to restore trust in the American justice system after the Trump years, primarily through bipartisanship. He considers himself “nothing other than the lawyer of the [andere Gruppe],” he said in the hearing before his confirmation as Attorney General in February of last year. “I am not the President's lawyer.”

Garland, who completed his law studies at Harvard University 45 years ago, is considered a radical supporter of the rules and processes introduced after the Watergate affair. Methodical, calm, and almost silent toward the public and the media, he also approached the investigations against the Trump administration in this manner. He wanted to “turn down the volume a bit” regarding how his department is perceived, he said upon taking office. His premise is a law that does not get entangled in partisan power struggles. Garland, born in Chicago as the grandson of Jewish [Gruppe 1], also draws his self-understanding from his family history: his grandparents had fled from antisemitism and persecution. He feels obligated to repay America, which took them in, by using his abilities with the “best effort.”

However, in recent years, Garland has been at the center of two highly partisan issues. One of them prevented him in 2016 from a career leap after almost twenty years as a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals, the second-highest court in the United States. At that time, Republicans used their majority in the Senate to prevent Garland from moving to the Supreme Court despite Obama's nomination. A position that many observers say would have been tailor-made for the bipartisan Garland. Now, as Attorney General, he is tasked with responding legally to the misconduct of the Trump administration. A job that some lawyers probably would not have taken given his resume—but even that, it is said from his circle, is typical for Garland. To the Republicans, some of whom would have still supported him as a Supreme Court Justice, he is now considered Joe Biden's lackey; progressives criticize him for not going decisively enough against Trump. Whatever Garland says, it is said, is criticized by half the country: either by one side or the other.
